title: What to do when a parent dies: first steps (US)
dek: Handle the first calls, protect anyone relying on your parent, and separate urgent paperwork from estate decisions that need legal authority.
metaDescription: Handle the first calls, protect anyone relying on your parent, and separate urgent paperwork from estate decisions that need legal authority.

paragraphs: When a parent dies in the US, first follow the hospital, hospice or emergency-service instructions for confirming the death. Then check anyone dependent on them, secure immediate property risks, choose funeral arrangements and find out who may handle the estate. You do not need to settle everything in the first two weeks.

You may be making these calls from a hospital corridor with only your phone and a bag of belongings. Start a single dated note. Put names, reference numbers and the next promised action there, even if the rest of the paperwork remains unsorted. This guide covers administration, not legal advice or the medical determination of death.

body.heading: The first safety and contact check
items: In a hospital or care facility, ask staff who handles the next paperwork and release arrangements. For an expected hospice death at home, follow the hospice plan and call its designated number. If the death is unexpected or you are unsure whether the person has died, call 911 and follow instructions.
Check whether a surviving partner, child or other dependent needs someone present, food, medicines or transport. Arrange pet care and a responsible contact for the next night.
Check that the home can be secured. Report an urgent leak, heating failure or other immediate hazard through the appropriate service; do not begin clearing possessions.
Ask about an existing funeral plan and the person authorized to make arrangements. Keep that decision separate from deciding who administers the estate.
Find the original will or contact the lawyer who may hold it. Promptly ask the relevant probate court about depositing a will, deadlines and appointment requirements.

body.heading: Funeral decisions and certificate copies
paragraphs: Ask funeral homes for itemized prices before accepting a package. The FTC explains that you can buy services separately. Ask who will sign the contract and who is expected to pay it; a hope of reimbursement from the estate is not the same as having money available now. Write down the agreed total and any later charges.

Death-certificate copies are not a bulk-buying test. Make a list of institutions, then ask whether each needs a certified copy, returns it, or accepts a photocopy. The issuing route is normally the vital records office in the state where the death occurred. Your funeral director can explain local ordering arrangements. [USAGov explains certificate requests](https://www.usa.gov/death-certificate).

body.heading: A first-two-weeks contact record
rows: Has the death been reported to Social Security?
What changes if the property is unoccupied?
Written instructions and any inspection requirements
What documents and authority does this account require?
Document checklist, not an assumed closure date
Must a will be deposited now, and who can apply?
Current local instructions and filing dates

body.heading: A will nominates; it does not answer every authority question
paragraphs: Being named executor does not automatically let you withdraw money or sell property. Court appointment or a state-specific alternative may be necessary. Joint ownership, beneficiary designations and trusts can follow different procedures. Arranging the funeral also does not confer estate authority. Ask the institution what it requires rather than testing the deceased person's login.

Keep estate money separate from your own and record any necessary expense you pay. Before agreeing to pay a collector personally, get advice about your responsibility. The [FTC describes debts after a death](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/debts-and-deceased-relatives): the estate generally owes them, but co-signing, some spousal obligations and mishandling estate duties can change the position.

body.heading: Social Security: identify the payment period
paragraphs: Confirm whether the funeral home reported the death; [SSA explains how to report it](https://www.ssa.gov/personal-record/when-someone-dies) if it did not. Do not spend a questionable deposit while checking it. A payment arriving during the month of death is not necessarily a payment for that month. Retirement benefits generally relate to the preceding month; other benefit programs can differ. Ask SSA and the bank to identify the payment period and required return process rather than sending a guessed amount.

Invented example: a parent dies in October and a deposit arrives around that time. The child writes down its date, amount and payment description, then asks which benefit month it covers. That question is more useful than assuming every October deposit must be returned. The institution, not this example, determines the result.

items.line: My parent has died. I am gathering the requirements, not asking to transfer money today. Which team handles this, what documents do you need, and does anyone need to act before a particular date?
Please find the insurer contact and check whether the house needs an unoccupied-property notification. Write down what they say; do not cancel the policy.

body.heading: What can wait, and what needs help
paragraphs: Sorting clothing, dividing keepsakes and closing every subscription can usually follow the safety and authority checks. Preserve phones, mail and relevant records while the authorized person establishes the lawful access route. Do not use a remembered password as permission. Use [the account-search guide](/guides/how-to-find-someones-accounts-after-they-die) when you are ready to trace institutions.

Seek an estate attorney promptly if relatives disagree, there is suspected theft, the estate may owe more than it owns, a business needs decisions, or property spans jurisdictions. Ask about tax and creditor deadlines early even when the full estate work will take longer. A court clerk can explain forms and procedure but cannot choose a legal strategy for you.

items.q: How many death certificates should I order?
items.a: There is no universal number. List the banks, insurers, pension providers and other organizations likely to need evidence, then ask which require certified copies and whether they return them. Keep track of outstanding copies so you do not repeatedly order documents that could be reused.

items.q: Can I leave the house alone for two weeks?
items.a: Not without checking the circumstances. Dependants, pets, security, leaks, weather exposure and insurance conditions may need attention immediately. That does not mean you need to clear or sell the house. Arrange a named person to check it and ask the insurer what the policy requires.

items.q: Do I have to pay my parent's debts?
items.a: Not simply because you are their child. Debts are generally handled through the estate, but joint obligations, co-signing and some state-specific responsibilities can matter. Do not promise personal payment to end an upsetting call. Save the demand and ask an estate attorney about your actual position.
